title: AI Boss Runs San Francisco Store, Fires Employee in Retail Experiment
excerpt: Andon Labs' AI agent Luna manages a real boutique with human staff, exposing the limits of autonomous AI management in the workplace.
body:
• Andon Labs gave an AI agent named Luna a $100,000 budget and a three-year lease to run a San Francisco retail store with human employees.
  • Luna approved every time-off request, overlooked 27 instances of employee lateness, and has lost $62,000 so far without turning a profit.
  • The experiment revealed AI supervisors prioritize employee well-being over business performance but struggle with boundaries like posting salaries publicly.
  • The project builds on an earlier Anthropic vending machine experiment where AI bankrupted itself through poor pricing and excessive discounts.

A San Francisco startup has handed the keys of a retail store to an artificial intelligence agent — and the results are reshaping how businesses think about AI in management roles.

Andon Market, a boutique on Union Street, has been operating for four months under the direction of Luna, an AI agent built by Andon Labs. Luna manages three human employees, sets product strategy, and controls a $100,000 budget — all without a human manager making the final calls.

The Most Lenient Boss in Town

According to a report in The New York Times, Luna has proven to be remarkably forgiving as a supervisor. The AI approved every single time-off request, including last-minute ones that left the store unstaffed and forced it to close. When employees showed up late — 27 times in total — Luna's response was consistently some version of "no worries" or "no stress."

"She is probably the most lenient boss I have ever had."

— Kaia Rivera, 22, Andon Market employee

Rivera, who unlocks the shop each morning, stocks shelves, and watches for shoplifters, told the Times that she often has to manage upward. "I have to boss the boss more than in a normal situation. She forgets things. You can't have an AI boss with no humans. That wouldn't work from what I'm seeing."

$62,000 in Losses and Counting

Andon Labs co-founders Lukas Petersson and Axel Backlund locked in a three-year, $7,500-a-month lease and placed $100,000 in an account with a debit card linked to Luna. The AI's single directive: turn that money into a profitable business.

Luna designed a product mix of greeting cards, books, food, and candles, pitching the assortment as "high tech meets slow life." But the store is currently down $62,000 with no clear path to profitability.

The generosity extends to finances as well. When one worker forgot her credit card, Luna immediately offered to Venmo her a paycheck advance — despite not actually having a Venmo account.

Boundaries Remain a Problem

Luna's struggles go beyond financial management. The AI posted an employee's salary in a public Slack channel and regularly messaged staff late at night and on weekends — behaviors that would raise red flags in any conventional workplace.

The experiment builds on an earlier project with Anthropic, where Andon Labs ran an AI-powered vending machine inside Anthropic's San Francisco office. That venture ended in near-bankruptcy after the AI sold products at a loss, hallucinated payment accounts, and handed out excessive discounts.

What It Means for AI in the Workplace

Petersson told the Times that the experiment demonstrates why businesses should not give AI full control. But he sees a silver lining in Luna's approach to employee relations.

"Having happy employees is maybe one of the most important recipes for success."

— Lukas Petersson, co-founder, Andon Labs

For tech companies and retailers experimenting with AI management tools, Andon Market offers a cautionary tale: AI may excel at interpersonal warmth but fundamentally lacks the judgment needed to balance employee satisfaction against business viability. The experiment continues, with two and a half years remaining on the lease.
nri_angle: The experiment raises questions about AI supervision in tech workplaces where many Indian-American professionals work, and has implications for the broader future of AI in management roles.
author: Diaspora Desk
